title: Dawah Guide
subtitle: A gentle, step-by-step companion for sharing Islam with wisdom and kindness.
audienceNote: This is a private, direct-link guide for da'ees (those inviting to Islam). It is a field companion, not a script. Real conversations are not linear — listen first, move at the other person's pace, and leave the result to Allah.
reviewNote: Quran and hadith references were checked against online source links on 2026-06-03. This is not marked verified because qualified scholar/manual approval is still pending.
tonePrinciples: Invite with wisdom and good manners, never pressure.
Listen more than you speak. Ask one question at a time.
Never mock another person's beliefs or background.
Avoid debate for the sake of winning. Aim for understanding.
Keep the door open even if the conversation ends without Shahada.
Make sincere dua privately and leave the outcome to Allah.

start.title: Start the conversation
start.summary: Begin warmly and naturally. Build a genuine connection before discussing belief.
explanation: There is no perfect opening line. A sincere smile, a kind word, and real interest in the person matter more than any technique.
Let the conversation flow. You are not delivering a lecture — you are having a human conversation that may, gently, turn toward the purpose of life and our relationship with our Creator.
conversationTips: Make dua before you begin and ask Allah to soften both hearts.
Ask open questions and genuinely listen to the answers.
Ask permission before moving into a deeper topic: "Would it be okay if I shared how Islam looks at that?"
Find common ground first — most people care about truth, justice, and meaning.

believe-in-god-initial.title: Do they believe in God?
believe-in-god-initial.summary: Gently understand where the person stands. There is no right or wrong answer here — just a starting point.
conversationTips: Ask without judgment: "Do you believe in a Creator?" and let them explain in their own words.
If they are unsure, that is completely fine — meet them where they are.

options.label: Yes, they believe in God
options.helperText: Move toward understanding the Oneness of God.
options.ariaLabel: Yes, they believe in God — continue to Tawheed

options.label: No, or they are unsure
options.helperText: Gently explore the signs of creation together.
options.ariaLabel: No or unsure — explore the signs of creation

signs-creation-infinite-regress.title: The signs of creation
signs-creation-infinite-regress.summary: Invite them to reflect on the order, design, and existence of the universe — without forcing a conclusion.
explanation: Everything we see has a beginning and a cause. Reflecting on creation invites a simple question: did all of this come from nothing, or does it point to a Creator?
Share these reflections humbly, as wonder rather than as a debate to be won. The goal is to open a door to thought, not to corner anyone.
conversationTips: Invite reflection: "Have you ever wondered where everything ultimately came from?"
Use everyday examples of design and order rather than complex philosophy.
Stay calm and curious. Avoid turning it into an argument.
avoid: Overconfident philosophical claims you cannot explain.
Talking down to the person or implying they are foolish.

believe-in-god-after-signs.title: After reflecting, do they believe in God?
believe-in-god-after-signs.summary: Check in gently. Belief is between them and Allah — your role is only to invite.

options.label: Yes, they now believe
options.helperText: Move toward the Oneness of God.
options.ariaLabel: Yes, they now believe — continue to Tawheed

options.label: No, not yet
options.helperText: Close warmly and keep the door open.

tawheed-surah-ikhlas.title: The Oneness of God (Tawheed)
tawheed-surah-ikhlas.summary: Introduce who God is in Islam: One, Eternal, without partner or equal, as described in Surah Al-Ikhlas.
explanation: In Islam, God (Allah) is One — He has no partner, no children, and nothing is comparable to Him. "Allah" is simply the Arabic word for the One God, the same God worshipped by all the prophets.
Surah Al-Ikhlas is a short chapter of the Qur'an that summarizes this pure belief beautifully in four lines.
conversationTips: Explain that "Allah" is not a different God, but the One Creator of all.
Share Surah Al-Ikhlas as a gentle, clear summary of who God is.

one-god-initial.title: Do they accept that God is One?
one-god-initial.summary: See whether the idea of one, indivisible God resonates with them.

options.label: Yes, they accept One God
options.helperText: Move toward revelation, justice, and the Day of Judgement.
options.ariaLabel: Yes, they accept One God — continue

options.label: No, or they have questions
options.helperText: Gently discuss why multiple gods leads to contradiction.
options.ariaLabel: No or questions — discuss the logic of One God

ayat-ikhtilaf.title: Why One God makes sense
ayat-ikhtilaf.summary: Discuss, calmly, how multiple competing gods would lead to conflict and disorder — while a single Creator explains the harmony we observe.
explanation: If there were many gods with their own wills, creation would be pulled in conflicting directions. The order and harmony of the universe instead point to a single Authority.
Present this as a reflection, not as a knockout argument. Some people need time, and that is okay.
conversationTips: Keep the tone reflective and humble, never combative.
Allow silence and questions. You are planting a seed, not closing a sale.
avoid: Mocking polytheistic or other beliefs.
Turning the discussion into a heated debate.

one-god-after-ikhtilaf.title: Does One God make sense to them now?
one-god-after-ikhtilaf.summary: Check in again, gently and without pressure.

options.label: Yes, it makes sense now
options.helperText: Move toward revelation, justice, and the Day of Judgement.
options.ariaLabel: Yes — continue to revelation and the Day of Judgement

options.label: No, not yet
options.helperText: Close warmly and keep the door open.

justice-day-judgment-test-revelation.title: Justice, the test of life, and revelation
justice-day-judgment-test-revelation.eyebrow: Justice / Day of Judgement / Test / Revelation
justice-day-judgment-test-revelation.summary: Explain that this life is a test, that justice will be fulfilled on the Day of Judgement, and that God did not leave us without guidance.
explanation: A just God would not leave wrongdoing unaddressed forever. The Day of Judgement is where perfect justice is finally established.
Because life is a meaningful test, God sent revelation — guidance through His messengers — so we are never left to figure out the purpose of life alone.
conversationTips: Connect to their innate sense of justice and fairness.
Frame revelation as a mercy: we are not left guessing.

angels.title: Belief in the angels
angels.summary: Introduce the angels as honored creations of God who carry out His commands, including delivering revelation.
explanation: Angels are beings created by God from light, who never disobey Him. They have roles such as conveying revelation, recording deeds, and more.
Belief in the angels is part of the broader Islamic understanding of the unseen.

messengers-prophets.title: The messengers and prophets
messengers-prophets.summary: Explain that God sent many prophets and messengers across history, all carrying one core message: worship the One God.
explanation: From the first human being onward, God sent guides to every people. Names like Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus are deeply honored in Islam.
Though their communities and times differed, their central message was the same: there is only One God worthy of worship.
conversationTips: Emphasize the shared thread between the prophets — this often resonates with people of other faiths.

jesus-peace-be-upon-him.title: Jesus, peace be upon him
jesus-peace-be-upon-him.summary: Speak about Jesus with deep love and respect, as Islam honors him as one of the greatest messengers of God.
explanation: Muslims love and honor Jesus (peace be upon him). We believe in his miraculous birth, his miracles by God's permission, and his noble message.
Islam teaches that Jesus was a mighty messenger of God who called people to worship the One God. Approach this topic with great care and respect, especially with those of a Christian background.
conversationTips: Lead with shared love and respect for Jesus — never with criticism.
Listen carefully; this can be an emotional subject for many.
avoid: Disrespecting Christian beliefs or arguing aggressively about theology.
Rushing this conversation — give it warmth and time.

shahada-readiness-initial.title: Are they ready for the Shahada?
shahada-readiness-initial.summary: Sense whether the person feels ready to embrace Islam. Readiness must come from them, sincerely and freely.
conversationTips: Never pressure. Shahada must be a free, sincere choice.
Ask once with gentleness, then give them space to think.
It is completely fine — and often better — for someone to take more time.

options.label: Yes, they feel ready
options.helperText: Connect them with guidance and the community.
options.ariaLabel: Yes, they feel ready — connect them with community

options.label: Not yet
options.helperText: Encourage gently and keep the door open.

encourage-keep-door-open.title: Encourage gently, keep the door open
encourage-keep-door-open.summary: Offer warmth, resources, and friendship without any pressure. Let them know the door is always open.
explanation: Reassure them there is no rush and no pressure. Offer to answer questions any time, share a small number of trustworthy resources, and let them decide whether they want to continue now or later.
A kind, patient da'ee who keeps the door open is far more effective than one who pushes. Guidance is from Allah, and many people accept Islam long after the first conversation.
conversationTips: Offer your contact and a few gentle resources.
If they look tired, tense, or overwhelmed, pause instead of adding more points.
Reaffirm the friendship regardless of their decision.
Make sincere dua for them privately.

shahada-readiness-after-encouragement.title: After encouragement, are they ready?
shahada-readiness-after-encouragement.summary: Only check in again if the moment still feels welcome. Whatever they decide, respond with kindness.

options.label: Yes, they ask to continue
options.helperText: Connect them with guidance and the community.
options.ariaLabel: Yes, they ask to continue — connect them with community

options.label: Still not yet
options.helperText: Close warmly and keep the door open.

connect-guidance-community.title: Connect them with guidance and community
connect-guidance-community.summary: Help them take the next steps with support. A new Muslim should never feel alone.
explanation: Embracing Islam is a beginning, not an ending. The most important thing now is loving support and gentle, practical guidance.
Help them connect with a trustworthy local community so they can learn and grow at their own pace.
checklist: Introduce them to a kind local imam or mentor.
Connect them with a new Muslim support group.
Help them find a welcoming local masjid.
Agree on a gentle follow-up plan (a check-in, a class, a meal together).
Share beginner-friendly resources on prayer and the basics of Islam.

respectful-exit-best-of-luck.title: Close warmly — keep the door open
respectful-exit-best-of-luck.summary: End every conversation with kindness, regardless of the outcome. Your job is to convey, not to convert.
explanation: Thank them sincerely for their time and openness. Make it clear they are always welcome to continue the conversation later.
Avoid any frustration or debate. Guidance is from Allah alone — your role is only to invite with wisdom and good manners, and to make dua for them privately.
conversationTips: Leave them with a good impression of Islam and Muslims.
Offer to stay in touch and to answer questions any time.
Do not ask for a decision after they have clearly paused or declined.
Make sincere dua for them after you part.

gorap.title: God
gorap.explanation: Establish belief in a Creator — the existence of God.

gorap.title: One God
gorap.explanation: Establish the Oneness of God — that He is One, without partner or equal.

gorap.title: Revelation
gorap.explanation: Establish that life is a test, justice will be fulfilled, and God sent revelation as guidance.

gorap.title: Angels
gorap.explanation: Establish belief in the angels, honored creations who carry out God's commands.

gorap.title: Prophets & Messengers
gorap.explanation: Establish belief in the prophets and messengers, who all carried one core message.

outsideTheField.title: Dua
outsideTheField.body: Make sincere dua for the person and for yourself before, during, and after the conversation. Guidance comes from Allah.

outsideTheField.title: Sincerity
outsideTheField.body: Purify your intention. You are conveying the message for the sake of Allah, not to win or to be seen.

outsideTheField.title: Planning
outsideTheField.body: Learn the basics well so you can answer common questions calmly and honestly. It is fine to say "I don't know, let me find out."

outsideTheField.title: Istiqamah
outsideTheField.body: Be steadfast and consistent in your own practice. Your character is your most powerful dawah.

onTheField.title: Make dua
onTheField.body: Quietly ask Allah to soften hearts as the conversation unfolds.

onTheField.title: Maintain a smile
onTheField.body: A warm, genuine smile is a form of charity and opens hearts.

onTheField.title: Be polite & kind
onTheField.body: Good manners leave a lasting, positive impression of Islam.

onTheField.title: Avoid unnecessary debate
onTheField.body: Aim for understanding, not for winning arguments. Step back if it becomes heated.

onTheField.title: Follow the flow & priorities
onTheField.body: Meet the person where they are. Don't force the order — let the conversation breathe.

onTheField.title: Be concise (time-aware)
onTheField.body: Respect their time and attention. Say less, listen more.

onTheField.title: Redirect to priorities
onTheField.body: Gently steer side-tangents back to the heart of the matter when helpful.

onTheField.title: Encourage Shahada (never force)
onTheField.body: Invite gently. The decision must be sincere and free. Never pressure anyone.

communityConnect.title: Connecting a new Muslim
communityConnect.intro: Whether someone takes their Shahada today or simply wants to keep learning, warm support matters most. Use this checklist to help them feel welcomed and never alone.
checklist: Introduce them to a kind, knowledgeable local imam or mentor.
Connect them with a new Muslim support group or class.
Help them find a welcoming local masjid near them.
Agree on a gentle follow-up — a check-in, a shared meal, or a class.
Share beginner-friendly resources on prayer and the basics of Islam.

trainingCards.title: Listening first
trainingCards.summary: A good dawah conversation begins with understanding the person, not with correcting them.
practice: Ask one open question and let them answer fully before responding.
Reflect back what you heard: "So it sounds like your main concern is..."
Answer the question they actually asked, not every topic you wish to cover.
avoid: Interrupting to win a point.
Assuming their background or objection before they explain it.

trainingCards.title: Ask permission before continuing
trainingCards.summary: Permission keeps the conversation respectful and helps the other person stay in control of their pace.
practice: Use simple phrases like: "Would it be okay if I shared the Islamic view?"
If they say no or hesitate, thank them and pause.
Offer to continue another time without making them feel guilty.
avoid: Treating hesitation as a challenge.
Repeating the same invitation after they clearly declined.

trainingCards.title: One point at a time
trainingCards.summary: Most people need one clear idea to think about, not a full lecture.
practice: Choose the next most relevant point in the conversation.
Use short explanations and pause for questions.
If several topics come up, write them down and return to one at a time.
avoid: Overloading them with every proof, ruling, or story you know.
Moving to Shahada before the person has processed the basics.

trainingCards.title: Handling hostility calmly
trainingCards.summary: If someone becomes angry or insulting, protect the dignity of the conversation and step back.
practice: Lower your voice and slow the pace.
Name the limit gently: "I do not want us to argue or disrespect each other."
End the conversation if it is no longer sincere or safe.
avoid: Matching anger with anger.
Using sarcasm, mockery, or public embarrassment.

trainingCards.title: When to stop the conversation
trainingCards.summary: Stopping well can be better dawah than forcing one more point.
practice: Stop when the person is tired, distressed, mocking, unsafe, or clearly done.
Make dua privately and leave the door open for a better time.
avoid: Chasing a decision.
Treating the conversation as a failure because it ended without Shahada.

trainingCards.title: Refer to an imam or mentor
trainingCards.summary: A da'ee does not need to answer everything. Sensitive, detailed, or personal questions need qualified help.
practice: Say clearly: "I do not want to guess about that."
Offer to connect them with a trusted local imam, teacher, or new Muslim mentor.
For emotional safety, legal, medical, or family-risk concerns, point them to qualified local professionals too.
avoid: Inventing rulings on the spot.
Becoming the person's only support after Shahada.

postShahadaHandoff.title: First hour
postShahadaHandoff.summary: Respond with warmth, privacy, and calm support. Shahada is a beginning, not a public performance.
actions: Congratulate them gently without overwhelming them.
Ask whether they want privacy, a quiet witness, or a public community introduction.
Write down one trusted contact: imam, mentor, new Muslim class, or supportive Muslim friend.
Check whether family, housing, work, or safety concerns make public disclosure risky.
avoid: Pressuring them to announce publicly.
Handing them a long list of rules immediately.
Posting photos, videos, or the Shahada moment without explicit permission.

postShahadaHandoff.title: First day
postShahadaHandoff.summary: Help them leave the conversation with one clear next step and one reliable support person.
actions: Share one beginner resource instead of a pile of links.
Offer to help them find a local masjid or new Muslim class.
Ask whether they want help learning wudu and the shape of prayer.
Remind them that learning takes time and Allah knows their effort.
avoid: Correcting every habit at once.
Debating family, marriage, clothing, or food details before they ask.

postShahadaHandoff.title: First week
postShahadaHandoff.summary: Support consistency, belonging, and safe learning before advanced rulings.
actions: Help them choose a gentle prayer-learning plan.
Connect them with a mentor who can answer questions patiently.
Invite them to one community moment: class, prayer, meal, or coffee.
Encourage them to ask sensitive questions privately and early.
avoid: Making yourself their only support.
Using shame to speed up their learning.

postShahadaHandoff.title: Connect to local community
postShahadaHandoff.summary: A new Muslim needs reliable people around them, not only online content.
actions: Introduce them to a trustworthy imam, teacher, or convert-support lead.
Help them verify class times and whether the space is beginner-friendly.
Offer a follow-up plan that respects their schedule and privacy.
If their family situation is tense, prioritize safety and trusted professional support.
avoid: Assuming every masjid has the same culture or support level.
Sharing their story without permission.

postShahadaHandoff.title: Avoid overwhelming them
postShahadaHandoff.summary: The first season after Shahada should feel supported, not buried under demands.
actions: Prioritize belief, prayer on-ramp, trustworthy community, and emotional steadiness.
Use short check-ins: one question, one resource, one next step.
Tell them clearly what can wait until a teacher reviews it with them.
Celebrate effort without making perfection the condition of belonging.
avoid: Turning the first week into a complete fiqh curriculum.
Making cultural changes sound like immediate religious obligations.

referralBoundaries.title: Marriage, divorce, and family law
referralBoundaries.summary: Do not improvise answers about marriage validity, divorce, custody, inheritance, conversion certificates, or family-law consequences.
examples: They ask whether their current marriage changes after Shahada.
They ask about divorce wording, custody, or inheritance.
They need documents for marriage, Hajj/Umrah, school, work, or government records.
referralBoundaries.referTo: A qualified local scholar and, where legal rights or documents are involved, a licensed legal professional or official agency.

referralBoundaries.title: Trauma, abuse, or safety risk
referralBoundaries.summary: If disclosure could lead to harm, do not encourage public action before safety has been considered.
examples: They fear violence, homelessness, stalking, or family retaliation.
They have trauma connected to religion or authority figures.
They ask whether they should tell unsafe relatives immediately.
referralBoundaries.referTo: Trusted local safety professionals, crisis or domestic-violence support, and a gentle imam or mentor who respects privacy.

referralBoundaries.title: Mental health crisis
referralBoundaries.summary: A da'ee should not try to counsel a crisis alone.
examples: They mention suicide, self-harm, being unable to stay safe, or feeling detached from reality.
They are panicking, unable to function, or making urgent unsafe plans.
They need emergency help more than a religious explanation.
referralBoundaries.referTo: Emergency services or crisis support such as 988 in the United States and Canada, plus qualified clinical care.

referralBoundaries.title: Detailed fiqh
referralBoundaries.summary: Worship and daily-life rulings can depend on school, circumstances, health, and local context.
examples: They ask about prayer validity, missed prayers, fasting exemptions, zakat calculations, purity details, or disability accommodations.
They ask for a ruling on food, work, clothing, family obligations, or money.
You are relying on memory rather than a reliable source.
referralBoundaries.referTo: A qualified scholar, imam, teacher, or trusted fatwa service that can ask follow-up questions.

referralBoundaries.title: Complex theology and disturbing claims
referralBoundaries.summary: Some questions need time, context, and a teacher rather than a quick answer.
examples: They ask about suffering, qadar, hellfire, hadith doubts, or difficult online claims.
They have trauma from previous religious communities.
They are spiraling through debate clips or hostile media.
referralBoundaries.referTo: A reliable teacher, structured class, or qualified scholar who can answer gradually and responsibly.

referralBoundaries.title: Legal, immigration, workplace, or school issues
referralBoundaries.summary: Religious encouragement cannot replace legal or official advice.
examples: They ask about immigration, asylum, custody, workplace rights, school accommodation, or ID documents.
They need a certificate, letter, or official proof.
They may face discrimination or retaliation.
referralBoundaries.referTo: A licensed legal professional, official public-rights agency, school/work office, or local settlement service as appropriate.

commonQuestions.question: How do you know God exists?
answer: Invite reflection rather than argument. Everything around us — the order of the universe, the precision of nature, our own existence — points to a Creator. Ask gently: did all of this come from nothing, or does it point to a Maker?
Stay humble. You are not trying to win; you are opening a door to thought.

commonQuestions.question: Why must God be one?
answer: If there were many gods with competing wills, creation would be pulled in conflicting directions. The harmony and order we observe instead point to a single Authority.
Present this as a reflection, and allow time and questions.

commonQuestions.question: What do Muslims believe about Jesus?
answer: Muslims love and deeply honour Jesus, peace be upon him. We believe in his miraculous birth to the Virgin Mary, his miracles by God's permission, and his noble message.
Islam teaches that Jesus was one of the greatest messengers of God, who called people to worship the One God. Approach this topic with warmth and respect.

commonQuestions.question: Why do we need prophets and scripture?
answer: Because life is a meaningful test, a just and merciful God did not leave us to guess our purpose. He sent guidance through messengers across history, all carrying one core message: worship the One God.
Revelation is a mercy — we are never left alone.

commonQuestions.question: What exactly is the Shahada?
answer: The Shahada is the sincere testimony that there is no god worthy of worship except Allah, and that Muhammad is His messenger. It is the gateway into Islam.
It must be a free, sincere choice — never rushed or pressured. Taking the Shahada is a beginning, not an ending; loving support comes next.

commonQuestions.question: If God is just, why is there suffering?
answer: This life is a test, and a just God will establish perfect justice on the Day of Judgement, where no wrong goes unaddressed.
Acknowledge the person's pain honestly and gently, rather than offering quick answers.

misconceptions.claim: Islam was spread by the sword.
response: The Qur'an is clear that faith cannot be forced — it must be sincere and freely chosen. Respond calmly and without defensiveness.
Point gently to the long history of communities embracing Islam by conviction, and keep the focus on the message rather than on debate.
"Allah" is simply the Arabic word for the One God — the same God worshipped by Abraham, Moses, and Jesus. Arabic-speaking Christians and Jews also call God "Allah."
Surah Al-Ikhlas summarizes this pure belief: God is One, eternal, with no partner and nothing comparable to Him.
Avoid a heated debate. Listen first, acknowledge that culture and religion are often confused, and separate harmful cultural practices from Islamic teaching.
Speak about the rights Islam affirmed for women and the honour given to mothers, and let your own respectful character speak.

misconceptions.claim: All religions are basically the same, so why switch?
response: Affirm the shared values — compassion, justice, honesty. Then gently note that the religions also make distinct claims about God, and those differences matter.
Invite reflection without pressure: the goal is sincere conviction, not winning a point.

scenarios.summary: Someone who does not believe in God, or is unsure.
approach: Begin with the question of God's existence and the signs of creation.
Ask open questions and listen genuinely to their reasoning.
Keep the tone curious and humble, not combative.
watchFor: Turning reflection into an argument to be won.
Overconfident philosophical claims you cannot explain.

scenarios.summary: Someone who already loves God and Jesus, peace be upon him.
approach: Lead with shared love and respect for Jesus and the prophets.
Introduce the Oneness of God gently and with care.
Honour the emotional weight this topic can carry.
watchFor: Disrespecting Christian beliefs or arguing theology aggressively.
Rushing — give the conversation warmth and time.

scenarios.summary: Someone who believes there may be more to life but distrusts organized religion.
approach: Begin with their desire for meaning, healing, or connection.
Explain Islam as direct worship of the One Creator, not as surrender to a human institution.
Show how revelation gives shape to spirituality without removing sincerity.
watchFor: Dismissing their past experiences with religion.
Using too much insider language before trust is built.

scenarios.summary: Someone raised around Islam who feels disconnected from it.
approach: Reconnect them with the meaning and beauty behind the practices.
Avoid judgment about the past; focus on a gentle next step.
Offer companionship and small, achievable encouragements.
watchFor: Shaming or guilt-tripping, which pushes people away.

scenarios.summary: A relative or close friend asks about Islam with emotion, fear, or challenging assumptions.
approach: Protect the relationship before trying to answer every objection.
Acknowledge the concern and answer one point calmly.
If the question is sensitive or beyond your knowledge, offer to ask an imam or mentor together.
watchFor: Letting family pressure push you into guessing.
Replying to emotional pain with a lecture.

scenarios.summary: Someone open to Islam who needs more time.
approach: Reassure them there is no rush and no pressure.
Offer trustworthy resources and to answer questions any time.
Keep the friendship and the door open, and make dua for them.
watchFor: Any pressure that makes a future conversation harder.

scenarios.summary: Someone is interested in Islam but past religious harm makes trust difficult.
approach: Do not defend what harmed them or rush into explanations.
Ask permission before sharing anything religious, and let them set the pace.
Offer a safe, qualified support route if trauma, panic, abuse, or crisis is present.
watchFor: Using verses or hadith as a quick fix for trauma.
Pushing them toward authority figures before trust and safety are considered.
Trying to replace clinical or safety support with your own advice.

scenarios.summary: Someone fears losing family, housing, work support, or emotional safety if they become Muslim.
approach: Validate the fear and avoid telling them to disclose before they are safe.
Help them think through who is safe to tell and who should wait.
Connect them with a local mentor, imam, or safety professional if disclosure may cause harm.
watchFor: Treating secrecy as weakness when there may be real risk.
Pressuring a public Shahada, social media post, or immediate family announcement.

scenarios.audience: Person interested but afraid to say Shahada publicly
scenarios.summary: Someone sincerely believes but is afraid of public attention, family reaction, or being recorded.
approach: Reassure them that pressure and public performance are not the goal.
Offer to connect them privately with a trusted imam or qualified mentor.
Ask whether they want a quiet witness, a private conversation, or time to learn more.
watchFor: Recording or sharing their Shahada without explicit permission.
Making a public announcement sound like the condition of becoming Muslim.
Ignoring safety concerns around family or community reaction.

scenarios.audience: Person asks about women in Islam
scenarios.summary: Someone asks about dignity, rights, modesty, marriage, divorce, culture, or harm done to women.
approach: Listen first; the question may come from personal pain, not only curiosity.
Separate Islamic teaching from harmful cultural practices and real abuse.
Use reliable sources and refer detailed marriage, divorce, inheritance, or safety questions to qualified help.
watchFor: Dismissing lived experiences or answering with slogans.
Guessing about personal legal, marriage, divorce, or abuse situations.
Turning the conversation into gender-war debate.

scenarios.summary: Someone asks why a just and merciful God allows pain, grief, oppression, or personal loss.
approach: Acknowledge the pain before offering an answer.
Explain gently that Islam teaches life is a test and that ultimate justice belongs to Allah.
If the pain is immediate or traumatic, refer to qualified emotional or crisis support.
watchFor: Giving a neat answer while the person is grieving.
Debating instead of listening.
Missing signs of crisis, self-harm, or unsafe isolation.

scenarios.audience: Person asks about violence or media narratives
scenarios.summary: Someone asks whether Islam promotes violence, terrorism, forced conversion, or hostility toward others.
approach: Stay calm and do not become defensive.
Clarify that faith cannot be forced and that Islam upholds the sanctity of life.
Use reliable, reviewed resources for complex terms like jihad, war, and political violence.
watchFor: Trying to answer every geopolitical issue at once.
Sharing weak apologetic claims you cannot support.
Arguing with someone who only wants a public fight.

duas.title: For ease and an open heart
duas.arabic: رَبِّ ٱشْرَحْ لِى صَدْرِى وَيَسِّرْ لِىٓ أَمْرِى
duas.transliteration: Rabbi-shraḥ lī ṣadrī wa yassir lī amrī
duas.translation: My Lord! Uplift my heart for me, and make my task easy,

duas.title: Unsourced personal wording for sincerity
duas.translation: Unsourced personal wording, not a transmitted dua: O Allah, make my intention sincere and help me speak truthfully and kindly.

duas.title: Unsourced personal wording after the conversation
duas.translation: Unsourced personal wording, not a transmitted dua: O Allah, guide them to what is true and good, and guide me to humility.

duas.title: Remembering guidance belongs to Allah
duas.arabic: إِنَّكَ لَا تَهْدِى مَنْ أَحْبَبْتَ وَلَٰكِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَهْدِى مَن يَشَآءُ
duas.translation: You surely cannot guide whoever you like, but it is Allah Who guides whoever He wills.

quickReference.intro: A compact recap of the GORAP path, the conversation flow, and the heart of good dawah. Use it as a refresher before or during a conversation.
points: Invite with wisdom and good manners; never pressure.
Listen more than you speak, and ask one question at a time.
Ask permission before moving deeper, and pause when the person needs space.
Meet people where they are — real conversations are not linear.
Keep the door open even if the conversation ends without Shahada.
Make sincere dua and leave the result to Allah.
